question: What is the primary physiological state that characterizes asphyxia?

options.A: Oxygen deprivation and excess carbon dioxide
options.B: Complete cessation of cardiac electrical activity
options.D: Severe drop in core body temperature

explanation: Asphyxia literally means suffocation, where inadequate oxygen reaches the tissues while carbon dioxide builds up in the blood. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h1)

question: A patient trapped in a smoke-filled room experiences asphyxia primarily due to which factor?

options.A: Toxic gas displacement of oxygen and airway irritation
options.B: Rapid internal bleeding from thermal injuries
options.C: Complete physical blockage by solid food particles
options.D: Sudden electrolyte imbalance in the heart muscle

explanation: Inhalation of smoke and toxic gases reduces available oxygen and causes severe inflammation, impairing gas exchange in the lungs. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h1)

question: During which stage of asphyxia do involuntary muscle spasms and loss of consciousness typically occur?
explanation: As oxygen deprivation worsens in the brain, electrical activity becomes chaotic, causing muscle twitching and convulsions. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h2)

question: Why does the breathing rate initially increase during the early phase of asphyxia?

options.A: The brain intentionally cools itself down by venting hot air
options.B: Chemoreceptors detect rising carbon dioxide and stimulate the respiratory center
options.C: Skeletal muscles demand more physical movement to stay warm
options.D: The heart pumps faster to push out stored toxins from the lungs

explanation: Central and peripheral chemoreceptors sense high carbon dioxide and low oxygen, triggering the brain to increase breathing efforts. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h2)

question: Which physical sign is most characteristic of early oxygen deprivation in the skin and mucous membranes?
explanation: A bluish discoloration called cyanosis appears when deoxygenated hemoglobin increases in the superficial blood vessels. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h3)

question: Why does tachycardia eventually shift to bradycardia as asphyxia becomes more severe?

options.A: Peripheral blood vessels constrict to force blood directly into the brain
options.B: The patient falls asleep and metabolic demands naturally decrease
options.C: The heart muscle becomes profoundly hypoxic and fails to maintain a fast rate
options.D: Baroreceptors reset the baseline blood pressure to a normal resting level

explanation: Initial oxygen shortage causes the heart to beat faster, but prolonged hypoxia starves the cardiac muscle, leading to a failing heart rate. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h3)

question: What is the standard manual maneuver used to open the airway of an unconscious patient without spinal trauma?
explanation: The head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver lifts the tongue away from the back of the throat to open the blocked airway. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h4)

question: What should a nurse do first when encountering an unresponsive patient choking on a solid foreign body?

options.A: Administer an intravenous line for emergency drug delivery
options.B: Clear visible objects from the mouth and establish an airway
options.C: Position the patient flat on the bed with legs elevated
options.D: Draw blood samples for immediate arterial blood gas analysis

explanation: Restoring airflow by removing any visible obstruction and opening the airway is the absolute priority in asphyxia management. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h4)

question: What is a primary focus of nursing care immediately after a patient is resuscitated from asphyxia?

options.A: Discharging the patient home with oral maintenance drugs
options.B: Continuous monitoring of oxygen saturation and vital signs
options.C: Encouraging immediate physical exercise to rebuild strength
options.D: Restricting all fluid intake to prevent kidney overload

explanation: Post-resuscitation care requires close observation to catch unstable vitals or falling oxygen levels before they cause more damage. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h5)

question: Why are frequent neurological checks necessary during the post-resuscitation phase?

options.A: To evaluate how well the liver is processing waste products
options.B: To detect secondary brain injury and cerebral edema early
options.C: To measure how much pain medication the patient can tolerate
options.D: To check if the patient remembers the exact cause of choking

explanation: The period following severe oxygen deprivation can lead to brain swelling, making careful neurological tracking vital. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h5)
